stories.title: Supreme Court rejects Brinda Karat's bid to reopen the 'goli maaro' hate-speech clean chit for two BJP leaders
key_points: The Supreme Court **dismissed a review petition** filed by CPI(M) leader **Brinda Karat** against its own April ruling.
That April ruling gave a **clean chit** to BJP leaders **Anurag Thakur and Parvesh Verma** over 2020 Delhi election hate-speech allegations.
Justices **Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta** found **no error** in the earlier judgment and declined an open-court hearing.
Karat had cited **Election Commission orders** from January 2020 that found the speeches violated the Model Code of Conduct.
The case centers on the infamous **'goli maaro saalon ko' ('shoot the traitors')** slogan controversy from the 2020 Delhi campaign.
stories.background: During campaigning for the 2020 Delhi Assembly election, BJP leaders including Union minister Anurag Thakur and MP Parvesh Verma made speeches that critics said incited violence against a religious minority — including a crowd chant of 'goli maaro saalon ko,' or 'shoot the traitors.' The Election Commission at the time found the speeches breached the Model Code of Conduct and temporarily barred both men from campaigning. Years later, in April 2026, the Supreme Court ruled that the speeches did not disclose a 'cognisable offence' — meaning no crime serious enough to require police investigation without a magistrate's order — effectively clearing the two leaders of criminal liability.
stories.what_happened: Brinda Karat, a senior CPI(M) leader, had asked the Supreme Court to review its own April 29, 2026 judgment, arguing the Court reached its conclusion **without a detailed examination of the evidence** or full arguments on the merits of the alleged hate speech. She pointed to the Election Commission's own January 2020 findings that the speeches had the potential to **'aggravate existing differences and promote mutual hatred between religious communities.'** On Monday, a bench of Justices **Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta** dismissed the review plea, finding **no apparent error** in the original ruling and declining Karat's request for an open-court hearing — meaning the case was decided on paperwork alone rather than live arguments. The dismissal makes the April clean chit to Thakur and Verma final, with no further review avenue within the Supreme Court itself.
stories.why_it_matters: The ruling closes the door on criminal accountability for two senior BJP figures over speech the Election Commission itself once flagged as inflammatory — reinforcing how high a legal bar exists in India between speech that election regulators can penalize administratively and speech that courts will treat as criminal.
stories.ripple_effects: The decision is likely to be cited in future hate-speech cases as precedent for how narrowly courts interpret 'cognisable offence' thresholds, making similar prosecutions harder to sustain. It also reignites debate over whether India's laws adequately punish political speech that regulators themselves judge to be communally inflammatory.
stories.why_now: The dismissal is the final chapter of a review process Karat initiated shortly after the original April 2026 ruling, and it closes out a six-year-old controversy dating back to the 2020 Delhi polls.
stories.watch_next: Whether Karat or other petitioners pursue any further legal avenue, such as a curative petition — a rare, last-resort appeal within the Supreme Court.

key_terms.definition: A crime serious enough that police can investigate and arrest without needing a magistrate's prior approval — the bar the Court found wasn't met here.

The Election Commission's rulebook for parties and candidates during elections, covering things like hate speech and misuse of official machinery; violations bring administrative penalties, not criminal charges.

stories.the_lesson: An election regulator flagging speech as inflammatory and a court finding it criminal are two very different bars — administrative rules can be violated without any law being broken, which is why political accountability and legal accountability often diverge.

stories.title: RBI's rate-setting committee begins its 3-day meeting — markets bet on a fourth straight pause
key_points: The **Reserve Bank of India's Monetary Policy Committee (MPC)** began its bi-monthly meeting today, running **August 3-5**.
Governor **Sanjay Malhotra** will announce the decision at **10am on Wednesday**, followed by a press conference.
**68 of 72 economists** polled by Reuters expect the **repo rate held at 5.25%** — a fourth straight pause.
The RBI already raised its **FY27 inflation forecast to 5.1%** (from 4.6%) on rising input costs, even as growth is pegged at **6.6%**.
A hold would come even as **global peers have hiked rates** in response to Iran-war-driven inflation pressure.
stories.background: The repo rate is the interest rate at which the RBI lends to commercial banks — it's the central lever India's central bank uses to control inflation and growth; cutting it makes borrowing cheaper (stimulating the economy), while raising it cools inflation by making money more expensive. The RBI last cut rates by 25 basis points in December 2025, to the current 5.25%, and has held steady at its last three reviews since. This meeting lands against a backdrop of easing crude oil prices (helping the inflation outlook) but the recent US tariffs on Indian goods complicating the growth picture.
stories.what_happened: India's six-member Monetary Policy Committee, headed by RBI Governor **Sanjay Malhotra**, convened Monday for its scheduled three-day bi-monthly review, with the rate decision due at **10am on Wednesday, August 5**, followed by a 12pm press conference. A Reuters poll of 72 economists found **68 expect the repo rate held at 5.25%**, continuing the pause that began after December's 25-basis-point cut. The RBI had already lifted its FY27 retail inflation forecast to **5.1%** from an earlier 4.6% estimate, citing mounting input costs, while projecting real GDP growth of **6.6%** for the year. The decision comes as India's factory growth has cooled to a near five-year low even as industrial output posted its fastest pace in nearly two years in June — a mixed picture that gives the MPC little clear signal to move in either direction.
stories.why_it_matters: The repo rate shapes borrowing costs for everything from home loans to business credit across India's economy — a pause keeps EMIs (loan installments) and fixed deposit returns unchanged, directly affecting household budgets and business investment decisions.
stories.ripple_effects: A hold, if it materializes, would likely be read by markets as the RBI prioritizing inflation control over further stimulus, especially with crude oil prices easing (helping the import bill) but US tariffs threatening export-driven growth. Bond and equity markets typically move on any surprise deviation from consensus, and a hawkish tone in Wednesday's press conference could pressure the rupee and bond yields even without a rate change.
stories.why_now: The MPC meets on a fixed bi-monthly schedule, and this is the scheduled August review — its first since the new US tariffs on Indian goods took effect.
stories.watch_next: Wednesday's 10am decision and Governor Malhotra's press conference for any shift in tone on inflation or growth risks from tariffs.

key_terms.definition: The interest rate at which the RBI lends short-term money to commercial banks — the main tool it uses to control inflation and economic growth.
One-hundredth of a percentage point; a '25 basis point cut' means a rate cut of 0.25%.

stories.the_lesson: Central banks often hold rates steady not because nothing is happening, but because two opposing risks — cooling factory growth and rising import-driven inflation — cancel each other out, leaving 'wait and see' as the least risky move.
stories.market_link: A hold or hawkish tone from the RBI on Wednesday could move Indian bond yields, bank stocks, and the rupee; a surprise cut would likely boost rate-sensitive sectors like real estate and autos.

stories.title: ITC's profit falls 15.6% even as revenue jumps 27% — cigarettes-to-hotels giant flags West Asia disruption
key_points: ITC's **consolidated net profit fell 15.6%** to **₹4,508.79 crore** for the June quarter (Q1 FY27), down from ₹5,343.41 crore a year earlier.
Revenue rose sharply to **₹29,523.30 crore**, with gross revenue from sale of products and services at ₹29,409.82 crore — up nearly **28%** year-on-year.
The **revenue-up, profit-down** mismatch signals margins got squeezed even as sales grew.
ITC pointed to **volatile, higher crude oil prices** and **supply-chain disruption** linked to the ongoing conflict in **West Asia**, plus one-off effects from its Sproutlife Foods acquisition.
The results land in the middle of India's **busiest earnings week**, with over 600 companies — including LIC, SBI and Bharti Airtel — reporting through August 8.
stories.background: ITC is one of India's largest conglomerates, built originally on cigarettes but now spanning hotels, packaged foods, paperboard/packaging, and agri-business — its cigarette division has historically been a cash-generating anchor that funds expansion into these other, lower-margin businesses. As a heavyweight Sensex and Nifty constituent, ITC's quarterly results are watched as a bellwether for consumer demand and cost pressures across India's FMCG (fast-moving consumer goods) sector. This quarter's numbers are also harder to compare cleanly with last year because ITC recently folded in its acquisition of Sproutlife Foods, and because global crude markets have been unusually volatile due to the West Asia conflict.
stories.what_happened: ITC reported **consolidated revenue of ₹29,523.30 crore** and **net profit of ₹4,508.79 crore** for the quarter ended June 2026 (Q1 FY27), a **15.61% decline** in profit from ₹5,343.41 crore in the same quarter last year, even as gross revenue from products and services climbed nearly **28%** to ₹29,409.82 crore. Total income for the quarter came in at ₹30,179.01 crore. ITC attributed the profit squeeze to a combination of factors: the impact of its Sproutlife Foods acquisition affecting year-on-year comparability, and heightened uncertainty from the ongoing **conflict in West Asia**, which triggered a sharp rise and volatility in crude oil and crude-linked input prices along with broader trade and supply-chain disruptions. The results were released as part of India's heaviest earnings week of the quarter, with more than 600 companies reporting results between August 3 and 8.
stories.why_it_matters: When a company's sales rise nearly 28% but profit falls 16%, it's a clear sign that **costs grew faster than revenue** — in this case linked to volatile global oil prices spilling into input costs. For a bellwether stock like ITC, that's a signal worth watching for whether cost pressure is company-specific or a broader problem for India's consumer-goods sector this earnings season.
stories.ripple_effects: A profit miss at a heavyweight index constituent can weigh on the FMCG segment of the Sensex/Nifty even while the broader market rallies on falling crude prices elsewhere (as it did earlier today on Iran-related news). Investors will be watching other consumer-goods results this week — Hindustan Unilever, Nestlé India, and others — to see whether ITC's margin squeeze is an isolated story or a sector-wide trend.
stories.why_now: This is ITC's scheduled quarterly earnings release, landing in the busiest stretch of India's Q1 FY27 corporate reporting season.
stories.watch_next: Whether other large consumer and FMCG companies reporting this week show the same cost-margin squeeze, which would confirm a sector-wide trend rather than a one-off for ITC.

key_terms.definition: A company's total profit including all its subsidiaries and majority-owned businesses combined, not just the parent company alone.

stories.the_lesson: Revenue growth doesn't automatically mean profit growth — when costs rise faster than sales, a company can post record revenue and still deliver a profit decline, which is exactly what makes reading past the headline number matter.
stories.market_link: ITC is a heavyweight Sensex/Nifty constituent; a profit miss in its results could weigh on the FMCG basket even as the broader index rallies on falling crude prices.

stories.title: Assam's flood death toll passes 80 as over 2 lakh people remain displaced
key_points: Assam's flood death toll has climbed to at least **80**, with more than **2.12 lakh people** (212,000) affected across **eight districts**.
The worst-hit districts include **Golaghat, Sivasagar, Jorhat, Dhemaji and Nagaon**, spanning **437 villages** in 21 revenue circles.
Nearly **17,200 hectares of cropland** are underwater, threatening farmers already squeezed by an uneven monsoon.
The central government has sanctioned **₹379.35 crore** in relief funds for Assam, part of a wider package that also covers Gujarat, Maharashtra, Odisha, Himachal Pradesh and Arunachal Pradesh.
Industrialist **Gautam Adani** donated **₹11 crore** to the Assam Chief Minister's Relief Fund as rescue and rehabilitation work continues.
stories.background: Assam sits on the floodplain of the **Brahmaputra river** and its tributaries, and severe monsoon flooding hits the state most years between June and September as the river swells with rainwater from Assam itself and upstream in the Himalayas. This year's floods have been unusually deadly and prolonged, coming on top of separate flood and landslide emergencies already hitting Kerala and Himachal Pradesh this monsoon season. Assam Chief Minister **Himanta Biswa Sarma** has been personally coordinating relief and rehabilitation operations, including door-to-door outreach by state ministers in the worst-affected districts.
stories.what_happened: As of the latest official figures from Assam's Disaster Reporting and Information Management System, the flood death toll in the state has reached **80**, with **2,12,441 people** affected across **eight districts** — Golaghat, Sivasagar, Biswanath, Charaideo, Kamrup Metropolitan, Jorhat, Dhemaji and Nagaon. The flood emergency now covers **437 villages** across **21 revenue circles**, and floodwaters have submerged roughly **17,198 hectares** of agricultural land, wiping out standing crops in some of the state's most fertile farming belts. The Centre has sanctioned **₹379.35 crore** in disaster relief funds specifically for Assam, as part of a broader relief package that also allocated ₹500 crore each to Gujarat, Maharashtra and Odisha, ₹193.95 crore to Himachal Pradesh, and ₹44.55 crore to Arunachal Pradesh. Separately, **Gautam Adani** contributed ₹11 crore to the state's Chief Minister's Relief Fund. Rescue and relief operations remain active, with floodwaters receding in some areas but localized flooding and riverbank erosion persisting elsewhere.
stories.why_it_matters: Eighty deaths and over 200,000 displaced people is a large-scale humanitarian emergency happening largely outside the national spotlight, which has been dominated by Parliament's Monsoon Session and Kerala's separate landslide crisis. The crop damage also has knock-on effects for local food supply and farmer incomes in a state that's already among India's poorer regions.
stories.ripple_effects: Lost cropland means reduced local harvests and income for farmers already dealing with an uneven monsoon, which can push up local food prices and increase migration pressure toward Assam's cities. The scale of displacement also puts political pressure on both the state and central government to speed up relief disbursement and longer-term flood-control infrastructure.
stories.why_now: Assam's flood situation has been building since late July and the toll has continued climbing through the first days of August as relief agencies update casualty figures from newly reached areas.
stories.watch_next: Whether the death toll keeps rising as rescue teams reach cut-off villages, and whether fresh rainfall — as IMD alerts have warned for the wider region — worsens the situation again.

key_terms.definition: An Indian numbering unit equal to 100,000 — so "2.12 lakh" means 212,000.

stories.the_lesson: Recurring seasonal disasters like Assam's floods rarely make it to the top of the news cycle the way a single dramatic event does, even when the death toll and displacement are larger — sustained, slow-moving crises compete poorly for attention against sudden ones.
stories.market_link: Crop losses across Assam add to broader food-inflation worries the RBI is weighing at its rate-setting meeting this week.

stories.title: Rajya Sabha passes bill giving small businesses real teeth to force overdue payments — as opposition disrupts the House over Amit Shah
key_points: The **MSME Development (Amendment) Bill, 2026** passed the Rajya Sabha by voice vote, targeting India's chronic **late-payment problem** for small firms
A buyer challenging an arbitration award must now **deposit 75% of the amount** before a court will even hear their appeal
If that appeal drags on **past six months**, courts can order **at least 50% of the award** paid to the small business immediately
Unpaid awards become recoverable like **arrears of land revenue** — the same fast-track tool used to collect unpaid tax
MSMEs contribute **over 31% of India's GDP** and employ close to **39 crore people**, according to government data cited by ministers
stories.background: India's Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development Act, 2006 already required large buyers to pay small suppliers within **45 days**, with unpaid disputes going to state-level **Facilitation Councils** for arbitration. In practice, buyers routinely dragged out that process for years by challenging awards in court, starving small businesses of cash they were legally owed. Union MSME Minister **Jitan Ram Manjhi** introduced this amendment bill in the Rajya Sabha on **July 29** specifically to close that loophole, calling it "the need of the present time." The bill passed today, during the Monsoon Session of Parliament.
stories.what_happened: The Rajya Sabha passed the **MSME Development (Amendment) Bill, 2026** by voice vote on Monday. The bill makes arbitral awards in favour of small businesses **enforceable as arrears of land revenue** and recognises them as legally binding debt under the **Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code**, giving suppliers a much faster route to actually collect what they're owed. Buyers who want to challenge an award in court must first **deposit 75% of the awarded amount**, and if their case is still pending after **six months**, courts can direct that **at least half the award be released** to the MSME supplier right away. States also get more flexibility in how they staff their Facilitation Councils, and the bill mandates that these councils be properly resourced and digitised so cases don't pile up. The bill's passage happened even as opposition MPs kept up **sustained sloganeering** in the House, demanding Home Minister **Amit Shah** explain the police crackdown — including use of pellet guns — on students protesting a NEET paper-leak issue at Delhi's Jantar Mantar on **July 20**, and address separate allegations of donation theft at the Ram temple in Ayodhya. TMC's Sagarika Ghose and Congress chief Mallikarjun Kharge were among those demanding the Prime Minister and Home Minister address the House directly.
stories.why_it_matters: Delayed payments are one of the biggest killers of small Indian businesses — they choke cash flow, force MSMEs to take on expensive short-term debt, and can cascade into defaults and layoffs. By making an unpaid award as easy to enforce as an unpaid tax bill, the amendment is meant to make it far more expensive for large buyers, including government departments and big corporates, to simply sit on what they owe.
stories.ripple_effects: Banks and NBFCs that lend against MSME receivables may become more willing to lend if payment timelines become more predictable, while large corporates and public buyers that have historically delayed MSME payments now face real financial exposure if they contest awards. The disruption over Amit Shah's absence also signals that this Monsoon Session continues to see major bills pushed through with minimal debate amid unresolved opposition grievances — a pattern already seen this session with other bills.
stories.why_now: The bill was timed to this Monsoon Session as part of the government's ease-of-doing-business push, and its passage today came even as the same opposition uproar over Shah's absence — running for over two weeks — continued to disrupt proceedings.
stories.watch_next: Whether the Lok Sabha takes up and passes the bill next, and whether Amit Shah eventually makes the statement on the Delhi student-protest crackdown that the opposition has been demanding.

key_terms.definition: A binding ruling issued by an arbitrator instead of a court, settling a payment dispute — in this case, between a small business and the buyer who owes it money.
An old, powerful recovery method originally used to collect unpaid land tax, letting the government seize a defaulter's assets quickly without a lengthy civil lawsuit.
A state-level body where a small business can file a complaint against a late-paying buyer and get a fast, legally binding ruling instead of going through a slow civil court.

stories.the_lesson: A law is only as strong as its enforcement teeth — India already had a 45-day payment rule for small businesses, but without a fast, costly consequence for ignoring it, large buyers kept delaying anyway; turning an unpaid award into something as easy to collect as unpaid tax is what finally gives the rule real bite.
stories.market_link: Faster, harder-edged payment enforcement could ease working-capital stress for MSME-focused lenders and NBFCs, while raising compliance and cash-flow risk for large corporates and public-sector buyers that carry unpaid dues to small suppliers.

stories.title: Karnataka finally completes its Congress cabinet — with no woman minister and two resignations in protest
key_points: **19 of 20 cleared MLAs** were sworn in as ministers, taking Chief Minister **DK Shivakumar's council to its full strength of 34**
The expansion came **nearly two months** after Shivakumar became CM under Congress's internal power-sharing deal with Siddaramaiah
The new council has **zero women ministers** — the one woman on the approved list was dropped over a pending legal case on her seat
Berths were split along caste lines: **7 Lingayat, 5 Vokkaliga, 7 Scheduled Caste and 3 Scheduled Tribe** ministers
**Two Congress MLAs resigned party posts** after being left out, and several senior leaders were dropped entirely
stories.background: Congress swept back to power in Karnataka in 2023 on the strength of an internal deal: **Siddaramaiah would be Chief Minister first**, and hand over to his rival **DK Shivakumar roughly halfway through the five-year term**. That handover happened on **June 3, 2026**, when Shivakumar was sworn in with just 13 ministers — a skeletal team meant to be a placeholder. Filling the remaining berths meant satisfying competing claims from Karnataka's powerful **Lingayat and Vokkaliga** communities, Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe legislators, Muslim leaders, and MLAs from every region of the state, which is why the full expansion took two more months of negotiation.
stories.what_happened: On Monday, **Governor Thaawarchand Gehlot** administered the oath of office to 19 new ministers at a ceremony at **Lok Bhavan in Bengaluru at 5 pm**. The Congress high command had actually cleared **20 names**, but Bhatkal MLA Mankal S Vaidya was dropped at the last minute to accommodate senior leader S S Mallikarjun, and MLC Gayathri Shanthegowda — the only woman on the list — was held back over a **pending Supreme Court-linked dispute over her own Council seat**, leaving the cabinet with no woman at all. The final lineup gives Lingayats and Vokkaligas 7 and 5 berths respectively, creates a first-ever slate of 7 SC ministers spanning different sub-categories, includes 3 ST ministers, and hands 3 Cabinet posts plus a top legislative post to Muslim leaders. Senior leaders including H K Patil, Dinesh Gundu Rao, Lakshmi Hebbalkar and N S Boseraju were **dropped from the ministry entirely**. Alongside the ministers, **GS Patil was named Assembly Speaker**, AS Ponnanna Deputy Speaker, and Saleem Ahmed Chairperson of the Legislative Council. Within hours, at least **two Congress MLAs resigned their party organisational posts** in protest at being excluded, and Shivakumar publicly promised disappointed MLAs "future chances."
stories.why_it_matters: Karnataka is Congress's biggest, richest and most politically important state government — its only real power base among India's large states — so how smoothly Shivakumar manages this cabinet is being watched as a test of whether the party's unusual mid-term CM-swap experiment can actually hold together. A messy expansion with public resignations suggests the internal bargaining isn't over.
stories.ripple_effects: Ministries and files that were stuck for two months because Shivakumar was juggling multiple portfolios himself can now move again, which matters for investment decisions and welfare scheme rollout in a state that anchors India's IT and biotech industries. The all-male cabinet is likely to draw criticism from women's groups and opposition parties, and continued discontent among sidelined leaders could resurface as factional trouble for Shivakumar down the line, potentially affecting Congress's national standing given how few states it governs outright.
stories.why_now: The expansion had been pending since Shivakumar took over as CM on June 3, and today's date was fixed only after Congress's central leadership finally signed off on a caste- and region-balanced list following weeks of internal lobbying.
stories.watch_next: Whether Shivakumar allots portfolios to the new ministers in the next few days without further public friction, and whether more sidelined leaders resign in protest.

key_terms.definition: The team of ministers, led by the Chief Minister, who run a state government and are each put in charge of departments like health, home or finance.
A formal promise every minister must make before taking charge, including to keep cabinet discussions confidential — administered by the Governor, the Centre's ceremonial representative in the state.
Two of Karnataka's largest and most politically powerful caste communities; almost every state government carefully balances cabinet seats between them to avoid alienating either voter base.

stories.the_lesson: Power-sharing deals inside a single party can be just as fragile as a multi-party coalition — when many claimants compete for a fixed number of posts, satisfying one group's caste, regional or gender balance almost always means visibly disappointing another, and managing that discontent becomes a governance job in itself.

stories.title: Rahul Gandhi calls delimitation a 'BJP conspiracy' to strip Tamil Nadu of power — Congress backs him, BJP hits back
key_points: Gandhi calls the planned delimitation **'designed to disenfranchise'** Tamil Nadu
He urges **all parties**, especially in Tamil Nadu, to unite against it
Congress has now **officially backed** Gandhi's stand; BJP has hit back
Lok Sabha seat numbers have been **frozen since the 1971 Census**
Southern states fear losing **relative seat share** once the freeze lifts after the next census
stories.background: India's Lok Sabha (the lower house of Parliament) allocates seats to states roughly by population. Because southern states like Tamil Nadu succeeded early at slowing population growth — largely through better health and education outcomes — while northern states grew faster, a straight population-based reallocation would shrink the South's seat share and grow the North's. To avoid punishing states for good policy, Parliament **froze seat numbers based on the 1971 Census**, and that freeze has been extended repeatedly, currently due to lift after the first census conducted post-2026. 'Delimitation' is the technical term for this seat-redrawing exercise, and it has been a live political fear in the South for years, since losing seats means losing a say in national policy and funding.
stories.what_happened: Speaking in **Chennai on Saturday**, Congress's Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha, **Rahul Gandhi**, said the BJP-led Centre's planned delimitation exercise was **'designed to disenfranchise people and take away the political power of the people of Tamil Nadu,'** calling it a **'BJP conspiracy.'** He called on political parties nationwide — especially in Tamil Nadu — to unite in opposition, warning that anyone who backs delimitation would be 'betraying Tamil Nadu.' By Monday, **Congress had formally thrown its weight behind Gandhi's position**, while the **BJP hit back**, rejecting the characterization and defending the government's approach. The dispute centers on the fact that Lok Sabha seat numbers have been **frozen since the 1971 Census** specifically to stop faster-growing northern states gaining seats at the expense of southern states that slowed population growth — a freeze due to lift after the next census.
stories.why_it_matters: This isn't abstract — losing Lok Sabha seats means losing votes in Parliament, cabinet berths, and influence over national budgets and policy. A fight over delimitation touches the core bargain of Indian federalism: how much power the states, especially the more economically developed South, retain against the Centre.
stories.ripple_effects: Expect southern chief ministers (Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana) to increasingly coordinate opposition to delimitation, potentially forming a bloc ahead of the next general election. It could also become a flashpoint in Centre-state relations more broadly, feeding into existing north-south tensions over tax devolution and language policy.
stories.why_now: Gandhi's remarks came as he wrapped up a Congress training camp in Tamil Nadu, and the issue is gaining urgency because delimitation is constitutionally due to happen after the first census conducted post-2026 — meaning the political fight over the rules starts now, well before the actual redrawing.
stories.watch_next: Watch for whether Tamil Nadu's ruling DMK and other southern parties formally join Congress's opposition, and whether the Centre clarifies its delimitation timeline in Parliament's ongoing Monsoon Session.

key_terms.definition: The process of redrawing electoral constituency boundaries and reallocating the number of seats each state gets in Parliament, usually based on updated population data.

stories.the_lesson: When a country freezes political representation to protect a policy goal — like rewarding states for slowing population growth — the freeze itself becomes a political fight once it's due to end, because unwinding it always creates winners and losers.

stories.title: Lok Sabha passes bill to expand the Supreme Court from 34 to 38 judges
key_points: The **Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Bill, 2026** passed the Lok Sabha by voice vote today
It raises the sanctioned strength of judges from **33 to 37**, excluding the Chief Justice — taking the full court from **34 to 38**
The change follows an **ordinance the President promulgated in May 2026**, which this bill now formally enacts into law
More sanctioned judges means **more benches can sit at once**, not that any single case gets more judges
stories.background: India's Supreme Court has repeatedly had its judge count raised over the decades as its case backlog has grown — the court now hears an enormous volume of appeals and constitutional matters each year. This particular expansion was first put into effect quickly via a **presidential ordinance in May 2026** (a temporary law the government can issue between parliamentary sessions), and the Monsoon Session's job was to formally convert that ordinance into a lasting **Act of Parliament**. The bill amends the original **Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Act, 1956**.
stories.what_happened: The Lok Sabha (India's lower house of Parliament) passed the **Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Bill, 2026** by voice vote today, formally raising the court's **sanctioned judge strength from 33 to 37**, excluding the Chief Justice of India — taking the court's total possible complement from **34 to 38 judges**. The bill converts into permanent law an ordinance the President had already promulgated in May 2026, under which the additional judges may already have begun functioning. The bill still needs to clear the Rajya Sabha (upper house) to complete its passage through Parliament. Government ministers framed the move as necessary to help the court clear its backlog faster.
stories.why_it_matters: Sanctioned strength determines how many benches the Supreme Court can run simultaneously on any given day — not how many judges hear a single case — so this is fundamentally about **increasing the court's total hearing capacity** to work through its backlog faster.
stories.ripple_effects: A larger bench capacity could mean faster listing and disposal of pending cases across constitutional, civil, and criminal matters, though the real-world effect depends on how quickly the new judgeships are actually filled. It also renews attention on the judicial appointments process (the collegium system) that will select who fills the new seats.
stories.why_now: This is happening now because Parliament's Monsoon Session, which resumed today, needed to formally ratify the ordinance the President issued in May before it lapses.
stories.watch_next: Watch for the bill's passage through the Rajya Sabha to complete its journey into law, and for announcements on who is appointed to the new judgeships.

key_terms.definition: A law the Indian President can issue when Parliament isn't in session, which must later be formally passed by Parliament to remain in effect.
The maximum number of judges a court is legally allowed to have — distinct from how many are actually appointed at any given time.

stories.the_lesson: Expanding a court doesn't mean any single case gets decided by more judges — it means more cases can be heard in parallel, which is a capacity fix for backlogs rather than a change to how individual cases are judged.

stories.title: Sri Lanka Women wrap up a 2-0 T20I series sweep over Pakistan — with a whitewash decider today
key_points: Sri Lanka Women won the **1st and 2nd T20Is** (July 31 and August 2) to seal the series **2-0**.
In the 2nd T20I, they chased **178 in just 17.4 overs**, with **14 balls to spare**.
**Sanjana Kavindi** (46 off 24) was Player of the Match, backing skipper **Chamari Athapaththu's** in-form batting.
Sri Lanka have now chased down **two 170+ totals** in consecutive matches — a sign of real depth, not luck.
The **3rd and final T20I** in Dambulla today is a dead rubber, but Sri Lanka are chasing a clean **3-0 whitewash**.
stories.background: Pakistan Women, captained by **Muneeba Ali**, are on a tour of Sri Lanka playing a three-match **T20I series** against the hosts, led by veteran opener **Chamari Athapaththu**. Sri Lanka's batting unit has been the standout of the series so far, repeatedly chasing down big totals with room to spare.
stories.what_happened: Sri Lanka Women beat Pakistan Women by **six wickets** in both the 1st T20I (July 31) and the 2nd T20I (August 2) at the Rangiri Dambulla International Stadium, sealing the three-match series with a match to spare. In the second game, Pakistan posted **175/5**, built around a 48-run knock from opener **Shawaal Zulfiqar** and 45 from Muneeba Ali, but Sri Lanka chased it down comfortably, reaching **178/4 in 17.4 overs**. **Sanjana Kavindi's** 46 off 24 balls earned her Player of the Match. Pakistan's bowling attack has struggled to defend competitive totals against Sri Lanka's aggressive chasing across both matches. The two sides meet for the **series-ending 3rd T20I today**, with Sri Lanka aiming to complete a full 3-0 sweep.
stories.why_it_matters: Successfully chasing two targets over 170 in a row — against different bowling attacks and match situations — signals genuine batting depth for Sri Lanka Women rather than a one-off good day, useful form heading into bigger ICC tournaments.
stories.ripple_effects: A comprehensive series loss piles pressure on Pakistan Women's batting and bowling combinations ahead of their next assignments, while boosting confidence for Sri Lanka's core group of Athapaththu, Kavindi, and Imesha Dulani.
stories.why_now: The series concludes today with the third and final match in Dambulla.
stories.watch_next: Whether Sri Lanka completes the clean sweep in today's decider, or Pakistan salvages a consolation win.
stories.the_lesson: Chasing down a big target once can be luck; doing it twice in a row against different bowling attacks is a real signal of a team's form and depth.

stories.title: Welsh Fire chase down Southern Brave with five balls to spare in The Hundred
key_points: **Welsh Fire** beat **Southern Brave** by **6 wickets**, with 5 balls remaining, at Cardiff.
Southern Brave were restricted to **115/8** batting first.
Welsh Fire chased the target down, finishing on **116/4** off 95 balls.
The win keeps Welsh Fire firmly in contention as **The Hundred's** group stage nears its end.
The tournament's knockouts begin with the **Eliminator on August 14** and the **Final at Lord's on August 16**.
stories.background: **The Hundred** is England's 100-ball franchise cricket tournament, launched in 2021 to attract new fans with a shorter, simplified format than traditional T20 cricket. Eight city-based men's and women's teams compete each summer, with the top three finishers in the group stage advancing to the knockouts — the second- and third-placed teams play an eliminator, with the winner facing the top team in the final. **Welsh Fire**, based in Cardiff, and **Southern Brave** are two of the tournament's eight men's franchises.
stories.what_happened: **Welsh Fire** beat **Southern Brave** by **6 wickets** at Sophia Gardens in Cardiff on **August 3**, with 5 balls to spare. Batting first, Southern Brave were restricted to **115 for 8** in their 100 balls. Welsh Fire chased the target down comfortably, reaching **116 for 4** off 95 balls to seal the win. The result strengthens Welsh Fire's position as the group stage of the 2026 competition heads into its final rounds. The Hundred's knockout stage follows shortly after, with the **Eliminator on August 14** between the second- and third-placed teams, and the **Final at Lord's on August 16**.
stories.why_it_matters: Every group-stage result now carries extra weight, since only the top three of eight teams advance to the knockouts — a win like this can be the difference between a home final shot and an early exit.
stories.ripple_effects: A tighter race for the top three spots draws more attention, and broadcast interest, to the final rounds of group matches, and affects which overseas and England players get showcased in the more-watched knockout stage.
stories.why_now: This was a live group-stage fixture on the tournament's active August schedule, part of the run-in before the August 14 Eliminator and August 16 Final.
stories.watch_next: Watch the points table over the next week as the final group games decide which three teams reach the knockouts.

key_terms.definition: A knockout match in franchise cricket between the second- and third-placed teams, with the winner advancing to the final.

stories.the_lesson: In a short group stage, every match carries outsized weight — there's little time for a team to recover from a bad loss before the table locks in for the knockouts.

stories.title: Tilak Varma named South Zone captain as BCCI announces Duleep Trophy 2026-27 squads
key_points: India T20I vice-captain **Tilak Varma** will lead South Zone in the season-opening Duleep Trophy.
**Ricky Bhui** is named vice-captain, with veteran **Karun Nair** also included in the 15-man squad.
**Rajat Patidar** has been named captain of Central Zone for the tournament.
The tournament runs **August 23 to September 10** at the BCCI Centre of Excellence in Bengaluru.
It's a first competitive red-ball assignment for several contracted India players before the international season resumes.
stories.background: The **Duleep Trophy** is one of Indian domestic cricket's oldest first-class tournaments, contested between zonal teams (North, South, East, West, Central) and traditionally used by selectors to assess players' red-ball form outside the more famous Ranji Trophy. It's often a proving ground for fringe India players and a place for established internationals to sharpen their game between series. Handing an India T20I vice-captain like Tilak Varma a first-class leadership role signals selectors see him as a longer-term leadership prospect, not just a white-ball specialist.
stories.what_happened: The BCCI announced squads for the **2026-27 Duleep Trophy**, with **Tilak Varma**, India's T20I vice-captain, named captain of South Zone and **Ricky Bhui** as his deputy. The South Zone squad also features experienced batter **Karun Nair** alongside a mix of domestic regulars. Separately, **Rajat Patidar** was confirmed as Central Zone's captain for the tournament. The competition — one of Indian cricket's oldest first-class events — will be held at the **BCCI Centre of Excellence in Bengaluru from August 23 to September 10**, giving contracted players a red-ball tune-up before India's international season resumes with the Sri Lanka Test tour later in August.
stories.why_it_matters: Captaincy assignments in tournaments like the Duleep Trophy are closely watched signals of who selectors are grooming for future national leadership roles, especially in a period where India's leadership across formats has seen recent turnover. It also gives fringe and returning players a competitive red-ball platform ahead of a busy international calendar.
stories.ripple_effects: Strong performances in the tournament can fast-track uncapped or fringe players into India's Test or white-ball squads later in the year. The tournament also serves as a fitness and form check for players returning from injury or IPL-heavy schedules.
stories.why_now: The squads were announced as the tournament's August 23 start date approaches and as several India-contracted players wrap up other commitments, including the ongoing IPL-adjacent leagues and India's tour planning for Sri Lanka.
stories.watch_next: How Tilak Varma performs in a first-class leadership role, and whether any uncapped players force their way into national selection conversations during the tournament.

key_terms.definition: The traditional multi-day format of cricket (as opposed to limited-overs formats like ODIs or T20s), considered the truest test of technique and used to prepare players for Test cricket.

stories.the_lesson: Leadership opportunities in lower-profile competitions are often where organizations quietly test who they trust to lead at the highest level later.

stories.title: Harmanpreet Kaur keeps India Women's captaincy as BCCI names Asia Cup 2026 squad
key_points: BCCI announced a **15-member squad** for the 2026 Women's Asia Cup.
**Harmanpreet Kaur** retains the captaincy; **Smriti Mandhana** stays vice-captain.
Squad includes Shafali Verma, Jemimah Rodrigues, Deepti Sharma, and wicketkeeper **Richa Ghosh**.
India go in as **defending stakes-holders**, aiming to reclaim the continental crown.
A separate **India A squad** was also named for the ACC Rising Stars Asia Cup.
stories.background: The **Women's Asia Cup** is the region's top continental cricket title, contested by India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and other Asian sides. India has traditionally been the dominant side but has faced tougher competition in recent editions as rivals like Sri Lanka and Bangladesh have improved. **Harmanpreet Kaur** has captained India Women through a period of rising expectations, including a maiden T20 World Cup near-miss, while **Smriti Mandhana** remains the team's most consistent batting star.
stories.what_happened: The **BCCI (Board of Control for Cricket in India)** announced a **15-player squad** for the 2026 Women's Asia Cup, retaining **Harmanpreet Kaur as captain** and **Smriti Mandhana as vice-captain**. The full squad includes Shafali Verma, Jemimah Rodrigues, Bharati Fulmali, Deepti Sharma, wicketkeepers Richa Ghosh and G. Kamalini, Arundhati Reddy, Prema Rawat, Radha Yadav, Sree Charani, Renuka Thakur, Nandini Sharma and Kranti Gaud. The board separately named an **India A squad** for the ACC Rising Stars Asia Cup, a parallel tournament for emerging players, giving several uncapped players — including Radha Yadav as captain of that side — a shot at senior selectors' attention.
stories.why_it_matters: Squad announcements set the stage for how India will approach a tournament they're expected to win but haven't always dominated in recent years — continuity in leadership (Harmanpreet-Mandhana) signals the selectors are backing experience over a reset, even as depth gets tested through the India A pipeline.
stories.ripple_effects: Players named to the India A Rising Stars squad get a visible platform to push for full India selection; any strong showings there often shape squad changes for the following season's bigger tournaments, including future World Cups.
stories.why_now: The squad was announced within the last day, ahead of the tournament's build-up.
stories.watch_next: India's opening match schedule and squad fitness updates as the Asia Cup approaches.

key_terms.definition: The deputy leader of a cricket team, who takes over captaincy duties if the captain is unavailable and is often being groomed for the top job.

stories.the_lesson: Selectors often signal their strategy through continuity as much as through change — keeping the same captain and vice-captain shows a team trusts its current leadership core even while it experiments with fresh talent lower down the squad.

stories.title: Shafique and Babar Azam century stands haul Pakistan back into the 2nd Test after West Indies' 344

thread.previously: We reported West Indies had recovered to 239/5 on Day 2 at Queen's Park Oval, with Justin Greaves anchoring the innings against dominant Pakistani spin bowling.
thread.changed: West Indies were eventually bowled out for 344 (Greaves 73, Roston Chase 70, Sajid Khan 4/85). In reply, Pakistan's openers turned the game around: Abdullah Shafique made a century and Babar Azam batted his way to 86 not out, an unbeaten 168-run stand that took Pakistan to 266/2 at Day 2's close — just 78 runs behind, with the series on the line.

key_points: West Indies were bowled out for **344** — Justin Greaves (73) and Roston Chase (70) top-scored.
Pakistan's **Sajid Khan** took 4/85 with spin to help wrap up the innings.
**Abdullah Shafique** made his **sixth Test century** (107 not out) opening the batting.
**Babar Azam** was unbeaten on **86**, closing in on his first Test century in four years.
Shafique and Babar's unbeaten **168-run stand** left Pakistan just **78 runs behind** at Day 2's close.
stories.background: This is the **second and final Test** of Pakistan's tour of the West Indies, played at Port of Spain's **Queen's Park Oval** — a series-decider after the first Test finished level. **Babar Azam**, Pakistan's long-time talisman and former captain, has endured a well-documented **four-year century drought** in Test cricket, making this innings a personal comeback story as much as a team one. **Abdullah Shafique** has quietly become Pakistan's most reliable opener over the same stretch.
stories.what_happened: After Pakistan's bowlers dismissed West Indies for **344** — Justin Greaves (73) and Roston Chase (70) leading the recovery, with spinner **Sajid Khan** taking **4 for 85** — Pakistan's reply started shakily before Shafique and Babar Azam dug in. **Abdullah Shafique reached his sixth Test century (107 not out)**, while **Babar Azam batted to an unbeaten 86**, edging closer to what would be his first Test hundred in four years. Together they built an unbroken **168-run partnership** that carried Pakistan to **266 for 2** at the close of Day 2 — leaving them just **78 runs** behind West Indies' first-innings total with eight wickets still in hand, putting Pakistan firmly back in a series-deciding Test they needed to win.
stories.why_it_matters: With the series tied 1-1 after the first Test, this match decides the series outright — and Pakistan clawing back from a position of weakness, powered by Babar Azam's return to form, is exactly the kind of result that can define both a series and a struggling star's season.
stories.ripple_effects: A strong finish here would ease pressure on Babar Azam's place and form heading into Pakistan's next assignments, while a West Indies collapse in the field would raise fresh questions about their bowling depth outside the pace attack.
stories.why_now: Day 2 concluded on August 3 with this dramatic swing in momentum, setting up a pivotal Day 3.
stories.watch_next: Whether Babar Azam converts his overnight 86 into a full century on Day 3, and whether Pakistan can push for a first-innings lead.

key_terms.definition: In a Test match, the side that scores more runs in its first turn at bat gains a psychological and tactical edge for the rest of the game.

stories.the_lesson: In Test cricket, a match can flip completely within a single session — being behind after Day 1 or Day 2 means far less than it looks like at the time.

stories.title: Aiden Markram plays down talk he'll be named Lucknow Super Giants' next IPL captain
key_points: **Aiden Markram** downplayed speculation he'll take over as **Lucknow Super Giants (LSG)** captain for the next IPL season.
The captaincy question opened up after **Rishabh Pant** stepped down and was **traded to Delhi Capitals** for Kuldeep Yadav.
Markram said 'the thoughts haven't been there just yet' and pointed to **other 'quality leaders'** in the squad.
Australia's T20I captain **Mitchell Marsh**, also on LSG's roster, is seen as the other obvious contender.
Markram is South Africa's own **T20 captain**, making him a natural favorite despite his reluctance to commit.
stories.background: Rishabh Pant had captained Lucknow Super Giants, but he was traded to Delhi Capitals in exchange for spinner Kuldeep Yadav, leaving the IPL franchise without a permanent leader heading into its next campaign. Markram, South Africa's white-ball captain, is widely regarded as a natural choice given his existing captaincy credentials, but LSG also has Australia's T20I captain Mitchell Marsh on its roster as an alternative option.
stories.what_happened: Asked directly about the vacant LSG captaincy on Monday, Aiden Markram said, **'I've got no idea,'** adding that the decision belongs to the franchise: **'They can decide whatever they think is best. There are some quality leaders in that group that we have there, so I'm not too fussed about it.'** He said 'the thoughts haven't been there just yet' on his own candidacy, despite being widely seen as a frontrunner given his experience captaining South Africa's T20 side. The vacancy opened after Rishabh Pant's trade to Delhi Capitals for Kuldeep Yadav left LSG without its previous leader. Mitchell Marsh, Australia's T20I captain and another senior figure in LSG's squad, is viewed as the other realistic contender for the role.
stories.why_it_matters: IPL captaincy decisions shape a franchise's on-field identity and tactical direction for years, and this appointment will be closely watched as one of the first major leadership calls of the post-Pant era at one of the league's higher-profile teams.
stories.ripple_effects: Whoever gets the armband affects LSG's leadership dynamic among a squad with multiple senior international captains, and the decision will likely factor into the league's ongoing pre-season trade and retention moves ahead of the next IPL auction cycle.
stories.why_now: The captaincy question has been open since Pant's trade earlier this year, and Markram's comments Monday are the first time he's addressed it directly in public.
stories.watch_next: Whether LSG announces a permanent captain before the next IPL season, and whether it's Markram, Marsh, or another squad member.
stories.the_lesson: In team sports, a leadership vacancy doesn't always get filled by the most obvious candidate — organizations often weigh squad dynamics and multiple qualified options rather than defaulting to reputation alone.

stories.title: Bangladesh's first Test tour of Australia in 23 years begins — without its fastest bowler
key_points: Bangladesh departed for Australia on **August 1**, starting its **first Test tour of Australia in 23 years**.
Strike pacer **Nahid Rana** is ruled out of the **entire two-Test series** with a Grade 2 side strain suffered against Zimbabwe.
Wicketkeeper-batter **Liton Das** will miss the **first Test** but is expected to be fit for the second.
The tour opens with a **three-day warm-up match** in Darwin (Aug 6-8), before the **first Test in Darwin from August 13** and the second in **Mackay from August 22**.
Uncapped fast bowler **Musfik Hasan** has been added to the squad in Rana's absence.
stories.background: Bangladesh has toured Australia for Test cricket only rarely, and this trip marks the team's **first Test tour there in 23 years** — a landmark for a side still building credibility in the format's toughest conditions. Australian pitches, with their extra pace and bounce, are traditionally the hardest challenge for subcontinent teams, making a fit, in-form fast-bowling attack especially important. Nahid Rana, Bangladesh's quickest bowler, sustained his injury during the second T20I against Zimbabwe on **July 17**, and the Bangladesh Cricket Board (BCB) confirmed on **July 25** that he would miss the tour entirely.
stories.what_happened: Bangladesh's Test squad departed for Australia on **August 1, 2026**, beginning what is the team's first Test tour of the country in **23 years**. The tour will not feature strike pacer **Nahid Rana**, who suffered a **Grade 2 side strain** during Bangladesh's second T20I against Zimbabwe on July 17 and has been ruled out of the entire two-match series. Wicketkeeper-batter **Liton Das** will also miss the opening Test, though he's expected to recover in time for the second. Uncapped quick **Musfik Hasan** has been named in the squad as cover. The tour schedule opens with a three-day warm-up match against a Cricket Australia XI at Darwin's DXC Arena from August 6-8, followed by the first Test in Darwin from August 13 and the second, and final, Test in Mackay from August 22.
stories.why_it_matters: A historic first tour in over two decades is a meaningful test of how far Bangladesh's Test team has progressed, but losing its best fast bowler before a ball is bowled significantly weakens its chances against Australia's traditionally pace-heavy home conditions.
stories.ripple_effects: Bangladesh will likely lean more heavily on its remaining seam and swing bowlers, and results here could shape selection and confidence heading into the team's next assignments in the World Test Championship cycle.
stories.why_now: The squad's departure and tour schedule are unfolding this week, with the warm-up match starting within days.
stories.watch_next: How Bangladesh's depleted pace attack performs in the Darwin warm-up match ahead of the first Test on August 13.
stories.the_lesson: A team's biggest test often arrives right when it's missing its most important player — depth in a squad matters as much as the star performers at the top of it.

stories.title: USA cricketer Akhilesh Reddy banned for eight years over Abu Dhabi T10 match-fixing
key_points: USA international **Bodugum Akhilesh Reddy**, 26, has been banned from all cricket for **eight years**.
The ICC's Anti-Corruption Tribunal found him guilty over conduct during the **2025 Abu Dhabi T10 League**.
He asked a teammate to **'give runs'** — deliberately concede extra runs while bowling — allegedly on behalf of team management.
That teammate refused and instead **reported him to the ICC's Anti-Corruption Unit**, and was dropped from the XI as a result.
Reddy also **deleted messages and call logs** from his phone in an attempt to obstruct the investigation.
stories.background: The **Abu Dhabi T10** is a short, fast franchise tournament in the UAE that has repeatedly drawn scrutiny from cricket's anti-corruption authorities, because its **compressed matches, lower player profiles and heavy betting-market interest** make it an attractive target for fixers looking for less scrutiny than bigger leagues get. The **ICC Anti-Corruption Unit (ACU)** monitors global franchise leagues for approaches to players, officials and support staff, and has banned other players and even support-staff members from past T10 editions. Reddy, an Indian-origin American cricketer, was **provisionally suspended in November 2025** while the ICC investigated, and the case has now concluded with a tribunal verdict finding him guilty.
stories.what_happened: The ICC's Anti-Corruption Tribunal found **Akhilesh Reddy** guilty on **three counts** of the Anti-Corruption Code over his conduct during the **2025 Abu Dhabi T10 League**. The tribunal ruled that he approached a teammate — referred to as 'Player A' — and asked him to **'give runs'**, meaning deliberately bowl in a way that concedes extra runs, allegedly at the behest of team management. When that player refused and instead reported the approach to the ICC's Anti-Corruption Unit, he was **dropped from the playing XI** shortly before the match in question. Reddy was also found to have **obstructed the investigation** by deleting relevant messages and call logs from his mobile phone once it began. His **eight-year ban is backdated to 21 November 2025**, the date of his provisional suspension, meaning he will not be eligible to return until **2033**.
stories.why_it_matters: This is a case where the player who was approached to fix a match **refused and reported it**, showing cricket's anti-corruption reporting system working as intended instead of a cover-up only being uncovered later. It also reinforces that **smaller, lower-profile franchise leagues** like the Abu Dhabi T10 remain a soft target for match-fixing in global cricket.
stories.ripple_effects: The ban effectively ends Reddy's career with **USA Cricket**, a program trying to build credibility as it grows the sport domestically after co-hosting the 2024 T20 World Cup. It may push tournament organisers and the ICC toward tighter oversight of shorter, lower-salary franchise leagues where the temptation to fix is higher. The tribunal's findings also reference a **'team management'** instruction Reddy says he was acting on, which could mean further action against others is still to come.
stories.why_now: The tribunal's verdict and the eight-year sanction were announced today, closing out an investigation that began with Reddy's **provisional suspension back in November 2025**.
stories.watch_next: Watch whether the ICC's investigation extends further up the chain to the team management Reddy claims directed him, and how USA Cricket responds to a contracted player being banned.

key_terms.definition: The rules that ban cricketers, coaches and officials from fixing matches or parts of matches, or helping others do so, enforced by the ICC's Anti-Corruption Unit.
An ultra-short format where each team bats for only 10 overs, so a full match finishes in around 90 minutes.

stories.the_lesson: Corruption in cricket is usually stopped not by outsiders catching a fixer, but by a player on the inside refusing a corrupt approach and reporting it — which is why anti-corruption systems are built around protecting whistle-blowing teammates.

stories.title: Punjab Kings vice-captain Shashank Singh quits Chhattisgarh for Puducherry over 'disrespect'
key_points: Shashank Singh, Punjab Kings' **vice-captain** and the **2023-24 BCCI best domestic white-ball all-rounder**, has left Chhattisgarh for **Puducherry**.
He was dropped from the **2026 Chhattisgarh Cricket Premier League** squad with **no explanation** given.
Singh says the state association gave him **no support** while he recovered from a shoulder injury and a fractured finger.
He will play **white-ball cricket only** this season while he keeps managing his fitness.
The **Chhattisgarh State Cricket Sangh** issued him a **No-Objection Certificate (NOC)** to make the move official.
stories.background: Shashank Singh spent most of a long domestic career representing **Chhattisgarh**, a relatively young state cricket association carved out after the state's 2000 formation, before an explosive **2023 IPL season with Punjab Kings** turned him into a household name and, eventually, the franchise's **vice-captain**. He was named the **BCCI's best domestic white-ball all-rounder for 2023-24**, one of Indian domestic cricket's more prestigious individual honours. Players switch states in Indian domestic cricket occasionally and always need a **No-Objection Certificate (NOC)** from their current association, but a contracted IPL player of Singh's profile walking away is unusual and signals a real breakdown in the player-association relationship, not a routine transfer.
stories.what_happened: Shashank Singh has left **Chhattisgarh** to represent **Puducherry** from the **2026-27 domestic season**, after the Chhattisgarh State Cricket Sangh (CSCS) issued him the NOC he needed to switch states. Singh told ESPNcricinfo the association gave him **no explanation** for excluding him from the **2026 Chhattisgarh Cricket Premier League** squad, and did not tell him why he was also missing from the **conditioning camp** for state probables. He said he had spent much of the past year managing a **shoulder injury and a fractured finger** and felt the board failed to support him through that recovery, adding that someone who won a **BCCI domestic award** deserves 'clarity, not ridicule'. Puducherry has agreed to let him play **white-ball cricket only** for now while he continues managing his fitness. The switch comes only months after Singh was made Punjab Kings' vice-captain in the IPL, raising his public profile just as his domestic-team relationship collapsed.
stories.why_it_matters: It is a rare, public breakdown between a **high-profile IPL player** and his home state association — the kind of selection dispute that usually stays behind closed doors in Indian domestic cricket. It highlights a real tension in the sport: state associations still control **Ranji Trophy and domestic league** selection, but IPL fame increasingly gives players enough leverage and options to simply leave if they feel mismanaged.
stories.ripple_effects: Chhattisgarh cricket loses one of its most recognisable modern players just as its own **Premier League** gets underway, raising uncomfortable questions about how the association manages injured or high-profile players. Puducherry, a smaller domestic side, instantly gains a proven IPL finisher for white-ball cricket. Other contracted IPL players watching a state board criticised in public may feel more confident seeking their own NOCs if they feel unsupported during injury layoffs.
stories.why_now: The move surfaces today because Indian domestic cricket's **2026-27 squad announcements** are being made this week, and Singh's exclusion from the Chhattisgarh Premier League squad was, in his telling, the final straw after months of being ignored by the association.
stories.watch_next: Watch whether the Chhattisgarh association responds publicly to Singh's comments, and whether he is named in a Puducherry white-ball squad in the coming weeks.

key_terms.definition: A formal clearance a player must get from their current state cricket association before they are allowed to represent a different state in Indian domestic cricket.
Cricket played between Indian states and regions, such as the Ranji Trophy, separate from the IPL — it's where most players build their reputation and fitness base.

stories.the_lesson: Even in a sport reshaped by IPL money, a player's week-to-week cricket future still runs through unglamorous state-association decisions — squad lists, fitness camps, medical support — and stardom doesn't exempt anyone from needing that relationship to actually work.

stories.title: Justin Greaves steadies West Indies to 239/5 as spin bowling dominates Day 2 in Trinidad
key_points: West Indies reach **239/5** with **5 wickets in hand** after Day 2
**Justin Greaves** unbeaten on a fighting half-century, an unbroken **66-run stand** with Roston Chase
Pakistan's spin pair **Usman and Sajid** stifled West Indies for long periods
Every West Indies batter reached **double figures** — no cheap wickets for Pakistan
This is the **series-deciding 2nd Test** at Trinidad's Queen's Park Oval
stories.background: Pakistan is touring the West Indies for a **two-match Test series**, with the second and final Test at Trinidad's Queen's Park Oval running **August 2-6**. Day 1 was disrupted by rain and marked by Pakistan's decision to drop veteran fast bowler **Mohammad Abbas**, with West Indies closing on **165 for 3**. Because this is the series decider, every session carries extra weight for both sides.
stories.what_happened: On **Day 2**, West Indies extended their overnight position to **239 for 5** by the time bad light stopped play, taking the upper hand on a spin-dominated day. **Justin Greaves** batted through the innings unbeaten for a fighting half-century, combining with **Roston Chase** for an unbroken **66-run partnership** that pushed the total past 200 with five wickets still in hand. Pakistan's spin duo, **Usman and Sajid**, bowled in tandem for long stretches and kept West Indies pinned down, but couldn't find the breakthroughs they needed — every West Indies batter in the lineup reached double figures, denying Pakistan the cheap dismissals needed to build pressure. Day 1 had already been disrupted by rain, during which Pakistan dropped seasoned pacer Mohammad Abbas from the XI, a call that drew scrutiny given his experience.
stories.why_it_matters: This is the decider in a two-match series, so the runs West Indies are banking now directly shape who wins the series. A modest, grinding total built on 'no cheap wickets' is often more valuable on a tricky, spin-friendly pitch than a flashy but fragile one.
stories.ripple_effects: A strong West Indies total puts pressure on Pakistan's own batting line-up, especially after the selection call to leave out an experienced bowler like Abbas. It also feeds into the ICC World Test Championship standings both sides are trying to climb.
stories.why_now: This is simply the natural progression of the match — Day 2 news follows Day 1, with the series-deciding stakes raising the profile of every session.
stories.watch_next: Watch whether West Indies can extend their lead further on Day 3, and how Pakistan's bowling attack — missing Abbas — copes without their most experienced seamer.
stories.the_lesson: In cricket, disciplined batting that avoids cheap dismissals — even without big, quick scoring — is often what wins low-scoring, series-deciding matches, since it denies the bowling side the wicket clusters that create momentum.

thread.previously: Day 1 was disrupted by rain, and Pakistan's decision to drop experienced seamer Mohammad Abbas drew scrutiny; West Indies closed on 165 for 3.
thread.changed: West Indies extended their position to 239 for 5, with Justin Greaves batting through for an unbeaten half-century and every batter reaching double figures against tight Pakistan spin.

stories.title: BCCI will keep paying Ajinkya Rahane a ₹70,000 monthly pension even after his retirement
key_points: Rahane qualifies for BCCI's **elite pension scheme** after playing **85 Tests, 90 ODIs and 20 T20Is** for India
He'll receive **₹70,000 a month** under the board's **2022-revised pension scheme**, up from ₹50,000 previously
The pension gets **suspended** if he takes a full-time BCCI role like coach or selector — but can resume if he later leaves that role
This follows his retirement from all international cricket, announced **July 30**
stories.background: The BCCI (Board of Control for Cricket in India) runs a **pension scheme for former international players** who meet career-length thresholds, as a form of long-term financial security once players stop earning central contracts and match fees. The scheme was **revised upward in 2022**, raising payouts for senior former players. Rahane retired from all formats of international cricket on **July 30, 2026** — a career that included being the hero of India's historic **2020-21 Border-Gavaskar Trophy win in Australia**, widely seen as one of Indian cricket's greatest overseas triumphs.
stories.what_happened: Days after Ajinkya Rahane announced his retirement from all international cricket, it's been confirmed he qualifies for the BCCI's **elite player pension scheme**, thanks to a long international career spanning **85 Tests, 90 ODIs, and 20 T20Is**. Under the board's **2022-revised pension structure**, he'll receive **₹70,000 per month** — up from the ₹50,000 top-tier former players received under the earlier scheme. There is one condition: if Rahane takes on a **full-time BCCI role**, such as a national or state coaching position or a selector's post, the monthly pension will be **temporarily suspended** for as long as he holds that job, and can resume once he leaves it.
stories.why_it_matters: The pension underscores how the BCCI, easily the world's wealthiest cricket board, has formalized long-term financial support for former internationals — a benefit far less common in cricket boards elsewhere in the world.
stories.ripple_effects: It reinforces the financial security net now available to India's senior retired cricketers, and may factor into other veteran players' retirement timing decisions. It also raises the question of whether Rahane will pursue a coaching or selection role next, which would pause the payments.
stories.why_now: This detail is emerging now as follow-up coverage to Rahane's retirement announcement on July 30, once outlets dug into what his benefits package actually looks like.
stories.watch_next: Watch for any announcement of a post-retirement coaching, mentorship, or selection role for Rahane, which would trigger the pension suspension clause.

key_terms.definition: A monthly payment the Board of Control for Cricket in India gives to former international players who meet career-length thresholds, as long-term financial support after retirement.

stories.the_lesson: Retirement benefits in sport aren't universal — they depend entirely on how wealthy and structured the specific league or board is, which is why the same career length can mean very different financial outcomes in different sports or countries.

thread.previously: Rahane announced his retirement from all formats of international cricket, capping a career defined by his heroics in India's historic 2020-21 series win in Australia.
thread.changed: It's now been confirmed he qualifies for BCCI's elite pension scheme and will receive ₹70,000 a month, with a clause suspending payments if he takes a full-time BCCI role.

stories.title: Ben Duckett becomes The Hundred's leading run-scorer as Trent Rockets edge SunRisers Leeds
key_points: **Trent Rockets** beat **SunRisers Leeds** by **5 runs** at Trent Bridge to stay top of the Men's Hundred table.
**Ben Duckett** smashed **64** off 47 balls, overtaking Phil Salt to become the competition's **leading run-scorer**.
**Aneurin Donald**, playing his first game of the tournament, blitzed a 19-ball **40 not out** with three sixes.
Pakistan pace veteran **Mohammad Amir** took 2 wickets for 20 runs in the death overs to seal the win.
Harry Brook fell for 46, caught by Duckett himself, as SunRisers fell 5 runs short chasing 147.
stories.background: The Hundred splits each match into 100-ball innings rather than the usual 120-ball T20 format, rewarding explosive hitting and tight death bowling. **Trent Rockets** have been one of the standout men's teams this season, and this was their third successive win, while **SunRisers Leeds**, led by Australian all-rounder Mitchell Marsh, came into the game looking to keep pace near the top of the table.
stories.what_happened: Batting first, Trent Rockets got a rapid start from **Aneurin Donald**, playing his first match of the campaign, who smashed **40 not out** off just 19 balls including three sixes. **Ben Duckett** then took over, reaching his third half-century of the tournament from 35 balls and adding a 50-run stand with Tim David before falling for **64** — a knock that made him the competition's leading run-scorer, overtaking England team-mate Phil Salt. Rockets posted **146 for 4**. In reply, Mitchell Marsh and Zak Crawley gave SunRisers Leeds a solid start, reaching 32 for 1 after the powerplay. Harry Brook threatened to take the game away before being caught by Duckett off Mohammad Amir for 46. Amir then struck twice more in the death overs, finishing with **2 for 20**, as SunRisers fell 5 runs short on **141 for 4**.
stories.why_it_matters: This result keeps Trent Rockets at the top of the men's table heading into the closing stages of the group phase, while individual milestones like Duckett's run-scoring lead feed into conversations about England white-ball selection and player value in franchise leagues worldwide.
stories.ripple_effects: Trent Rockets strengthen their claim to a top finish and a home knockout match, while SunRisers Leeds slip further off the pace despite Marsh and Brook's form. Duckett's red-hot Hundred form adds to the selection conversation around England's white-ball top order.
stories.why_now: The match was played on August 2, with reaction and reports still fresh as the tournament heads into its final week.
stories.watch_next: Watch whether Trent Rockets can maintain their unbeaten run and hold off SunRisers Leeds and other challengers as the race for the knockout stages tightens.

key_terms.definition: The opening overs of a limited-overs innings when fielding restrictions let batters attack more freely.
The final overs of a limited-overs innings, when bowlers try to defend a small target and batters try to maximize scoring.
The league standings that rank teams by wins, used to decide who reaches the knockout stage.

stories.the_lesson: In short-format cricket, a couple of quickfire cameos at the top of the order plus tight death bowling are often enough to win a game — and individual form in these leagues increasingly shapes international team selection.

stories.title: England's Danni Wyatt-Hodge ruled out of the rest of The Hundred with a calf tear
key_points: MI London's **Danni Wyatt-Hodge** ruled out of the remainder of the **Women's Hundred 2026** with a torn left calf.
The injury happened while she batted through pain for an unbeaten **52** against Southern Brave on July 27.
**Ella Claridge**, a 23-year-old USA international, has been signed as her replacement.
Wyatt-Hodge was MI London's joint-top run-scorer this season with **93 runs** at a strike rate of **132.85**.
MI London remain **winless** at the bottom of the table, now without one of their most in-form batters.
stories.background: The Hundred is England's short-format cricket competition where each team faces 100 balls per innings instead of the usual 120 in a T20. Danni Wyatt-Hodge is a veteran England international opening batter with over a decade of white-ball experience for her country. She plays for **MI London**, one of eight teams in the competition, who have struggled all season and sit **last** in the standings without a win. Losing an experienced international mid-season is a significant blow for a side already searching for answers.
stories.what_happened: Wyatt-Hodge picked up the injury while playing through discomfort during MI London's narrow loss to Southern Brave, where she still top-scored with an unbeaten **52**. Scans have since confirmed a **left calf tear**, ruling her out for the rest of the tournament. The Hundred has confirmed **Ella Claridge**, a 23-year-old batter who plays for the USA internationally and for The Blaze domestically, as her replacement in the MI London squad. The news follows fellow captain **Sophie Devine's** calf injury elsewhere in the competition, meaning two teams have lost key top-order batters to the same type of injury within days of each other. Wyatt-Hodge's 93 runs this season, at an average of 46.50, had made her one of the few bright spots in an otherwise winless campaign for MI London.
stories.why_it_matters: Losing a proven international batter mid-tournament forces a struggling team to rebuild its top order on the fly, right when it most needs experienced runs. It also underlines how the packed modern cricket calendar — leagues stacked back-to-back with international duty — is producing a steady stream of soft-tissue injuries like calf and hamstring tears.
stories.ripple_effects: MI London, already winless, must now find fresh runs at the top of the order from Ella Claridge, a new face in the competition, while chasing their first win of the season. stories.watch_next: Watch how Ella Claridge performs on her MI London debut and whether the team can find its first win of the season without Wyatt-Hodge.
